title: Шинковка и забывчивость  (Knife Skills and Forgetfulness)

segments.t: As German starts the evaluation with vegetable chopping at Claude Monet, Viktor puts on a theatrical display of forgetfulness at Arcobaleno until Elena feels guilty and lets him go. Listen to the Russian scene first.
У вас что-то горит, Виктор Петрович.
Глупая была идея, прости. Я тебя отпускаю.
Ты езжай, за меня не беспокойся. Я тут отдохну немножко.
Let's break this conversation down line by line.
'Viktor Petrovich, hand me a lemon, please.' Elena uses a polite everyday Russian courtesy expression that sets the tone of the conversation right away.
'Here you go.' Chef Barinov uses a polite everyday Russian courtesy expression that sets the tone of the conversation right away.
'I asked for a lemon.' Spoken Russian keeps this brief and expressive, built right around 'lemon' without extra helper words.
'Let's start with vegetable chopping.' German pairs 'let us begin' with 'vegetable' directly, since spoken Russian skips English filler words like 'the', 'a', and 'is'.
У вас что-то горит, Виктор Петрович.
'Something of yours is burning, Viktor Petrovich.' Russians say 'by me' or 'with us' where English says 'I have' or 'we have', without needing a separate word for 'have'.
'Viktor Petrovich, maybe you need some pills?' In spoken Russian, the words stay in their normal statement order and Elena's rising voice at the end turns the line into a question.
'Alas, there are no pills for old age.' In everyday Russian, 'alas' flows straight into 'pill, tablet' without extra linking words.
'This is my fault.' Elena uses the first-person pronoun in the case required by the Russian verb or preposition.
Глупая была идея, прости. Я тебя отпускаю.
'It was a foolish idea, forgive me. I am letting you go.' The past-tense verb ending marks the grammatical gender and number of the subject directly.
'Thank you.' Chef Barinov uses a polite everyday Russian courtesy expression that sets the tone of the conversation right away.
'I need to go to the market.' Russian expresses feelings and needs by saying 'to me it is needed' or 'to me it seems', putting the person in the 'to me' form.
Ты езжай, за меня не беспокойся. Я тут отдохну немножко.

'You go ahead, don't worry about me. I will rest here a little.' Chef Viktor addresses the listener with the informal singular pronoun, showing a close or familiar relationship. Now listen to the full Russian exchange again with everything in place.
У вас что-то горит, Виктор Петрович.
Глупая была идея, прости. Я тебя отпускаю.
Ты езжай, за меня не беспокойся. Я тут отдохну немножко.
That finishes Viktor's fake memory loss at Arcobaleno and Elena releasing him out of guilt. Notice how Russian expresses apologies and reassurance. Until next time!
